content_note: All items are ORIGINAL, authored for this project to stay license-clean. They are NOT real LSAT questions. schema ids reference speedrun/taxonomy/lsat_taxonomy.json. This is a small scaffold to exercise the pipeline; expand with a chosen licensed/original source before scoring.

items.stimulus: Employees who use the company's new standing desks report fewer afternoon headaches than those who use ordinary desks. Clearly, standing while working reduces headaches.
items.question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.text: Employees chose their own desks, and those prone to headaches avoided standing desks.
Standing desks are more expensive than ordinary desks.
Some employees with ordinary desks also report few headaches.
Afternoon headaches are more common than morning headaches.
Standing improves posture, which employees value.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C is 'too weak': a few headache-free ordinary-desk users is consistent with standing still helping on average. A attacks the causal link itself by offering a selection effect (a reverse-causation / self-selection alternative).

items.stimulus: Anyone who has mastered calculus can solve these puzzles. Maria solved these puzzles, so she has mastered calculus.
items.question: The reasoning above is flawed because it

choices.text: treats a condition sufficient for solving the puzzles as if it were necessary.
relies on the testimony of a single person.
fails to define what counts as mastering calculus.
assumes without warrant that the puzzles are difficult.
concludes that Maria cannot solve other kinds of puzzles.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: E describes a conclusion the argument never draws. A names the actual error: mastery is sufficient for solving, but the argument treats solving as sufficient for mastery (affirming the consequent).

items.stimulus: The new bridge will reduce commute times, so the city council should approve it: shorter commutes make residents happier.
items.question: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.text: The bridge will not create other problems that outweigh happier residents.
Every resident commutes across the river daily.
The bridge is the cheapest way to shorten commutes.
Residents have asked the council for a new bridge.
Happier residents always re-elect the council.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is 'too strong' — the argument needs some commute benefit, not that everyone commutes daily; negating B does not destroy the argument. A is required: if approving the bridge caused offsetting harms, the recommendation would collapse (negation test).

items.stimulus: Towns that added bike lanes saw retail sales rise. Adding bike lanes must boost local retail.
items.question: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.text: The towns added bike lanes without making any other economic changes during the period.
Bike lanes are popular with younger residents.
Retail sales also rose in towns without bike lanes.
Some retailers opposed the bike lanes.
Bike lanes reduce car traffic.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C actually weakens (a common cause raising sales everywhere). A strengthens by ruling out an alternative cause, protecting the causal claim.

items.stimulus: The clinic saw more patients this year than last, yet its total revenue fell.
items.question: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.text: This year the clinic shifted to shorter, lower-priced visits, seeing more patients for less money each.
The clinic hired two additional nurses this year.
Patient satisfaction scores rose this year.
The clinic is open the same hours as last year.
Nearby clinics also saw more patients.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: E is real-world plausible but says nothing about why THIS clinic's revenue fell. A resolves it: more visits at lower price per visit can lower total revenue.

items.stimulus: A magazine asked its readers to mail in whether they exercise daily; 80% said yes. So most people in the country exercise daily.
items.question: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.text: draws a conclusion about the country from a self-selected group of respondents.
assumes exercising daily is healthy.
reports that 80% of readers responded affirmatively.
fails to specify what counts as exercise.
ignores people who exercise weekly.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C merely restates a premise rather than naming an error. A identifies the sampling flaw: readers who mail in are not representative of the country.

items.stimulus: A larger percentage of Startup A's employees are managers than at giant Corp B. So Startup A has more managers than Corp B.
items.question: The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.text: infers a larger absolute number from a larger proportion.
assumes managers are more productive than other staff.
overlooks that Startup A is newer than Corp B.
treats being a manager as the same as being an executive, though it also ignores turnover.
assumes Corp B wants more managers.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: D is half-right/half-wrong (an equivocation clause plus an irrelevant turnover clause) and misses the point. A names the percentage-vs-number error directly: a bigger share of a much smaller company can be fewer people.

items.stimulus: Each part of this machine is lightweight, so the whole machine must be lightweight.
items.question: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that above?

choices.text: Every player on the team is excellent, so the team as a whole must be excellent.
This soup is salty, so each ingredient must be salty.
The report is long, so it must be thorough.
Since it rained yesterday, it will rain today.
All cats are animals, so some animals are cats.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is whole-to-part (division), the reverse direction. A matches the stimulus's part-to-whole (composition) error.

items.passage: Historians once treated early cartography as a straightforward record of geographic knowledge. Recent scholarship complicates this view. Maps, these scholars argue, were also instruments of persuasion: a ruler's map might exaggerate contested borders or omit rival settlements entirely. Yet the revisionists sometimes overreach, implying that accuracy was never a mapmaker's goal. The evidence suggests a middle position: cartographers pursued utility and rhetoric together, and the balance shifted with a map's purpose.
items.question: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.text: Early maps served both practical and persuasive purposes, in a balance that depended on their use.
Early maps were primarily tools of political propaganda.
Historians were wrong to study early cartography at all.
Revisionist scholars have corrected every earlier error about maps.
Accuracy was never a goal of early mapmakers.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B captures only the revisionist view the author qualifies; the author endorses the middle position (A), not persuasion as primary.

items.passage: (see rc-0001)
items.question: The author's attitude toward the revisionist scholarship is best described as

choices.text: partial agreement tempered by a specific reservation.
enthusiastic endorsement.
dismissive rejection.
complete indifference.
confusion about its claims.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: The author agrees the old view was too simple but says revisionists 'sometimes overreach' — a reservation, so partial agreement (A), not enthusiasm.

items.passage: (see rc-0001)
items.question: The reference to a ruler's map exaggerating contested borders functions primarily to

choices.text: illustrate the revisionist claim that maps could be persuasive.
prove that all maps are inaccurate.
introduce the author's own final position.
criticize rulers for dishonesty.
show that early historians were correct.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: The example supports the revisionist point being described, not the author's later middle position; C misattributes its function.

items.stimulus: People who sleep less tend to drink more coffee. Therefore, drinking coffee causes sleep loss.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.text: confuses a possible effect with a cause.
assumes all coffee drinkers sleep poorly.
fails to specify how much coffee is consumed.
relies on a sample of only coffee drinkers.
ignores the health benefits of coffee.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B overstates the conclusion; the error is reversed causation (A): poor sleep may drive coffee use, not the reverse.

items.stimulus: The team started wearing blue socks, then won three games in a row. The blue socks caused the winning streak.
items.question: The argument is flawed because it

choices.text: treats a sequence of events as proof of causation.
assumes the team will keep winning.
does not mention the team's coach.
overlooks that other teams also wear blue.
fails to define what counts as a winning streak.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: D is plausible but irrelevant; A names the post hoc error: temporal succession is not causation.

items.stimulus: Only members may use the pool. Jordan is a member, so Jordan must be permitted to use the pool.
items.question: The reasoning is questionable because it

choices.text: treats being a member, which is only a necessary condition for permission to use the pool, as if it were sufficient to guarantee that permission.
assumes the pool is open year-round.
fails to consider non-members who never swim.
confuses sufficient with necessary by inferring membership from permission to use the pool.
relies on a single instance.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: D describes the reverse inference (concluding membership from permission), which is actually valid; the argument instead treats membership as sufficient for permission, so A is correct.

items.stimulus: If the alarm had sounded, we would have evacuated. The alarm did not sound, so we did not need to evacuate.
items.question: The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.text: denies the antecedent and treats that as disproving the consequent.
assumes the alarm always works.
overlooks that evacuation can be warranted for other reasons.
confuses sufficient with necessary conditions.
relies on the testimony of one person.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C adds a plausible real-world caveat but the formal error is denying the antecedent (A): no alarm does not prove no need to evacuate.

items.stimulus: No study has proven that the supplement is harmful, so it is safe to take daily.
items.question: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.text: treats a lack of evidence as evidence of absence.
assumes all supplements are identical.
fails to recommend a dosage.
overlooks people who take the supplement weekly.
relies on anecdotal reports of benefit.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: E describes a different flaw; A is appeal to ignorance: unproven harm is not proof of safety.

items.stimulus: The law says no one may endanger the public interest. Publishing this article would interest the public, so it must be banned.
items.question: The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.text: uses 'interest' in two different senses.
assumes all articles endanger someone.
fails to define 'public'.
overlooks freedom of the press.
relies on a single law.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: D raises a policy concern; A identifies equivocation between public welfare and public curiosity.

items.stimulus: This policy is fair because it treats everyone the same, and it treats everyone the same because it is fair.
items.question: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.text: assumes in the premises what it tries to establish in the conclusion.
fails to define fairness.
overlooks policies that treat people differently.
relies on the opinion of policymakers.
assumes everyone wants equal treatment.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is a vagueness complaint; A names circular reasoning: fairness and equal treatment are used to prove each other.

items.stimulus: You cannot trust Dr. Lee's climate report — she drives a gas-powered car.
items.question: The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.text: attacks the person rather than the evidence offered.
assumes all scientists agree on climate.
fails to describe the report's methods.
overlooks electric vehicles.
confuses correlation with causation.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C asks for more detail but does not name the fallacy; A is ad hominem — personal behavior is irrelevant to the report's merits.

items.stimulus: My opponent wants to abolish all roads. Obviously we need some roads, so her transportation plan is absurd.
items.question: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.text: misrepresents the opposing view to make it easier to attack.
assumes roads are always necessary.
fails to consider rail transport.
relies on emotional language.
overlooks maintenance costs.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: Tone may be heated, but the core error is straw man (A): the opponent likely proposed reducing roads, not abolishing all.

items.stimulus: Either we ban all social media for teens or youth mental health will keep collapsing. We cannot ban all social media, so the collapse is inevitable.
items.question: The reasoning is flawed because it

choices.text: presents only two options when others may exist.
assumes social media is the sole cause of mental health problems.
fails to define 'collapse'.
overlooks adults' use of social media.
relies on a single expert.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B may be true but the structural flaw is false dilemma (A): regulation short of a total ban is a third path.

items.stimulus: The museum will exceed last year's attendance because it is hosting a major exhibit.
items.question: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion to follow logically?

choices.text: Nothing else will reduce attendance below last year's level.
Major exhibits always attract more visitors than minor ones.
Last year's attendance was a record.
The exhibit will run for six months.
Some visitors will come more than once.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is too strong and not required; A closes the gap: the exhibit must be enough net of any countervailing factors.

items.stimulus: All interns attend orientation. Some interns attend online orientation sessions, and no online session includes a lab tour.
items.question: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true?

choices.text: Some interns attend a session that does not include a lab tour.
All interns attend an online session.
No intern attends a lab tour.
Every orientation includes a lab tour.
Most interns prefer online orientation.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C overreaches; interns may still attend in-person sessions that include tours. A follows: the interns who attend online sessions attend a session with no lab tour.

items.stimulus: After the library extended its hours, evening visits rose sharply while daytime visits stayed flat.
items.question: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.text: The extended hours likely drew visitors who could not come earlier.
Daytime visitors no longer use the library.
The library should close during the day.
Every new visitor came only in the evening.
Extended hours reduced staffing costs.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: D is too strong; A is the modest inference that new evening capacity attracted a different crowd.

items.stimulus: Editor: We will not publish op-eds that cite unnamed sources on factual claims, because readers cannot verify them.
items.question: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the editor's decision?

choices.text: Publications should not present as fact what readers cannot check.
All op-eds should include at least two sources.
Unnamed sources are always unreliable.
Editors should publish controversial views.
Readers prefer named sources.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C is too absolute; A matches the verifiability rationale without banning all unnamed sources in every context.

items.stimulus: Critic: The director claims the film is historically accurate because she consulted archivists. But consulting archivists does not guarantee accuracy, since she may have ignored their advice.
items.question: The critic's argument proceeds by

choices.text: showing that a premise does not ensure the stated conclusion.
attacking the director's character.
offering an alternative film that is accurate.
proving the film is inaccurate.
appealing to popular opinion.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: The critic does not prove inaccuracy; A describes undermining the link between consultation and guaranteed accuracy.

items.stimulus: If the package arrives today, the lab can start the trial. The trial has not started, so the package did not arrive today.
items.question: Which one of the following exhibits reasoning most similar to that above?

choices.text: If it rains, the game is canceled. The game was canceled, so it must have rained.
Only members may vote. Sam voted, so Sam is a member.
If the gate is locked, we cannot enter. We entered, so the gate was not locked.
All dogs bark. This animal barks, so it is a dog.
The store is open unless it is a holiday. It is not a holiday, so the store is open.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: A affirms the consequent (the game was canceled, so it rained); the stimulus and the correct answer C deny the consequent to deny the antecedent (modus tollens).

items.stimulus: Some argue that remote work eliminates mentorship. That worry is overstated. Junior staff in our firm report more frequent check-ins with mentors than before, and retention has improved. Companies should therefore expand remote options rather than retreat from them.
items.question: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.text: Companies should expand remote work options.
Remote work eliminates mentorship.
Junior staff receive more check-ins than before.
The worry about mentorship is true.
Retention has improved in every company.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C is evidence supporting the conclusion; A is the recommendation the argument builds toward.

items.passage: Biologists long classified species mainly by visible traits. Molecular tools later revealed hidden divisions within groups that looked alike. Some researchers resisted the new taxonomy as impractical; others embraced it for conservation planning. The author argues that both views miss the point: classification should serve the question being asked, whether that is evolutionary history or field identification.
items.question: Which one of the following best describes the organization of the passage?

choices.text: A traditional view is described, a challenge is introduced, competing responses are noted, and a pragmatic resolution is offered.
Two scientific theories are compared and the second is rejected.
A problem is stated and three solutions are evaluated in detail.
Historical events are narrated in chronological order.
The author summarizes a single study's methods and results.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: The author does not reject molecular taxonomy; A captures the old view → challenge → debate → purpose-based resolution arc.

items.passage: (see rc-0002)
items.question: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would most likely agree that

choices.text: no single classification system is best for every biological purpose.
visible traits are useless for classification.
conservation planners should ignore molecular data.
researchers who resisted new taxonomy were simply lazy.
field identification and evolutionary history always coincide.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: The passage says the two can diverge; A follows from classification serving the question at hand.

items.stimulus: Principle: A policy should not burden a group unless it produces a compensating benefit to society.
items.question: Which situation most clearly violates the principle?

choices.text: A tax on textbooks funds schools but raises costs for low-income students without improving outcomes.
A toll funds road repairs that help commuters.
A subsidy helps farmers and lowers food prices.
A fee funds parks enjoyed by the payers.
A regulation protects workers and raises wages.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B has compensating benefit; A burdens a group without offsetting societal gain.

items.stimulus: The critic argues that the novel fails because its hero never changes; yet the hero's refusal to change is precisely what the author uses to critique society.
items.question: The argument responds by

choices.text: claiming a feature treated as a flaw serves the author's purpose.
denying that the hero exists.
appealing to popular opinion.
asserting all novels must have changing heroes.
attacking the critic personally.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: D invents a rule; A reframes the alleged flaw as intentional.

items.stimulus: If the server is down, emails queue. Emails are queuing, so the server is down.
items.question: Which argument has the most similar pattern?

choices.text: If it rains, the game is canceled. The game is canceled, so it rained.
If it rains, the streets get wet. It is raining, so the streets are wet.
Only members may park here. Sam parked here, so Sam is a member.
All dogs bark. Rex is a dog, so Rex barks.
The train is either early or on time. It is not early, so it is on time.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is valid reasoning (modus ponens: it is raining, so the streets are wet); the stimulus is flawed, affirming the consequent, a pattern only A shares.

items.stimulus: Since the river flooded twice this decade, and flood walls were never upgraded, the city should invest in levees now.
items.question: The main conclusion is that

choices.text: the city should invest in levees now.
the river flooded twice this decade.
flood walls were never upgraded.
levees always prevent flooding.
the decade is unusually wet.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is a premise; A is the recommendation (conclusion).

items.stimulus: The plan will fail unless costs fall. Costs have not fallen. Therefore the plan will fail.
items.question: The claim that costs have not fallen plays which role?

choices.text: It is a premise supporting the conclusion.
It is the main conclusion.
It is background context with no logical role.
It is an intermediate conclusion.
It contradicts the argument.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: D overstates; the statement is a direct premise, not a sub-conclusion.

items.stimulus: Alex: The policy reduced crime. Jordan: Crime fell everywhere this year, so we can't credit the policy.
items.question: Alex and Jordan disagree over whether

choices.text: the policy caused the local crime reduction.
crime fell locally.
crime is measurable.
policies ever work.
Jordan supports the policy.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: Both accept local decline; they dispute causation (A).

items.stimulus: The new curriculum improved test scores, so it should be adopted nationwide.
items.question: Which would be most useful to evaluate the argument?

choices.text: Whether other factors changed in the pilot schools at the same time.
Whether teachers liked the curriculum.
Whether students enjoy school.
Whether textbooks are expensive.
Whether the nation has many schools.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is tangential; A tests whether the curriculum caused the gain.

items.passage: (see rc-0002)
items.question: It can be inferred that the author would most likely agree that

choices.text: combining morphological and genetic data improves classification.
molecular tools should replace morphology entirely.
resistance to revision was entirely unreasonable.
visible traits are useless for biology.
the debate has been settled permanently.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: Author favors complementarity, not replacement (A).

items.passage: (see rc-0002)
items.question: The relationship between morphology-based classification and molecular classification is best described as

choices.text: initially sequential, later treated as mutually informative.
entirely unrelated disciplines.
identical in practice.
one disproving the other completely.
competitive with no overlap.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: Passage ends with complementarity; A captures historical then integrative relation.

items.stimulus: The witness saw a red car flee the scene, so the suspect's red car places him at the scene.
items.question: Which strengthens the argument?

choices.text: No other red cars were reported in the area that night.
The suspect owns a red car.
Red cars are common.
The witness wears glasses.
The suspect denies being there.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B could be true but doesn't strengthen identification; A reduces alternative red-car sources.

items.stimulus: Organic foods are healthier because they are natural.
items.question: Which weakens the argument?

choices.text: Many natural substances are harmful and many processed foods are safe.
Organic farming uses more land.
Consumers prefer organic labels.
Some organic foods taste better.
Farmers markets are popular.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: D is plausible but irrelevant to health; A attacks the natural=healthy assumption.

items.stimulus: A famous film star endorses this multivitamin, so it must be the most effective one available.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.text: relies on the endorsement of someone whose expertise is unrelated to nutrition.
assumes the multivitamin works equally well for everyone.
fails to specify what 'effective' means.
overlooks the price of the multivitamin.
restates that the star endorses the product.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B flags an overgeneralization, but the decisive defect is treating an irrelevant celebrity as an authority (A).

items.stimulus: A new textbook raised test scores at Lincoln High more than the old one did. So adopting it will raise scores at Kennedy High more than Kennedy's current book does.
items.question: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: assumes that what held at one school will hold at another that may differ in relevant ways.
presumes the old textbook was completely ineffective.
ignores the quality of teachers entirely.
concludes that every student's score will rise.
merely restates that scores rose at Lincoln.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C names one possible difference, but the general flaw is assuming the two schools are comparable at all (A); C is one instance, not the defect itself.

items.stimulus: No sweeping generalization is ever fully true. That, at least, is a claim we can assert with complete confidence.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: asserts a sweeping generalization with full confidence while denying any such claim can be fully true.
relies on a term it never defines.
provides too little evidence for its conclusion.
restates its premise as its conclusion.
could be true under some interpretations.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: It can look circular, but the precise defect is self-contradiction: the claim disqualifies itself (A), which is stronger than mere restatement.

items.stimulus: Neighborhoods with more coffee shops have higher home values. Clearly, opening coffee shops raises nearby home values.
items.question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.text: Developers deliberately open coffee shops in areas where home values are already climbing.
Some coffee shops close within their first year.
The city should approve more coffee-shop permits.
Property taxes tend to rise as home values rise.
A few high-value neighborhoods have very few coffee shops.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: E is too weak — a few exceptions don't undo an average trend; A supplies a reverse/common-cause alternative that attacks the causal claim directly.

items.stimulus: Students who report high confidence tend to score well on the exam. So building students' confidence will raise their exam scores.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: overlooks that scoring well may be what produces the confidence.
assumes confidence can be measured precisely.
concludes that every confident student scores well.
ignores students who lack confidence.
recommends a study schedule.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C attacks an overgeneralization the argument doesn't quite make; A identifies reversed causation, the actual gap.

items.stimulus: Children who take music lessons have better math grades. Therefore, music lessons improve mathematical ability.
items.question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.text: Families that can afford music lessons also tend to afford math tutoring.
Some talented musicians dislike mathematics.
Music and math both involve patterns.
Music lessons are expensive.
Schools should fund music programs.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B cites isolated exceptions (too weak); A introduces a common cause (family resources) explaining both variables.

items.stimulus: Right after the company introduced standing desks, sick days dropped. The standing desks must have made employees healthier.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: infers a causal link merely from one change following another in time.
assumes all employees used the standing desks.
fails to define 'healthier'.
ignores the cost of the desks.
restates that sick days dropped.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B raises a coverage worry, but the core error is post hoc reasoning — treating temporal sequence as causation (A).

items.stimulus: To pass the bar, you must study hard. Maria studied hard, so she will pass the bar.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: treats a necessary condition for passing as if it were sufficient.
assumes Maria wants to pass the bar.
concludes that everyone who studies passes.
ignores how long Maria studied.
restates that studying is required.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C describes a broader overgeneralization; the precise defect is confusing a necessary condition for a sufficient one (A).

items.stimulus: If a plant is a fern, then it reproduces by spores. This plant reproduces by spores, so it is a fern.
items.question: The flawed reasoning above is most similar to which one of the following?

choices.text: If a road is icy, it is dangerous. This road is dangerous, so it is icy.
If it rains, the game is canceled. It did not rain, so the game was not canceled.
All ferns are plants, and this is a fern, so it is a plant.
Most spore-bearers are ferns, so this is probably a fern.
Ferns are common, so many plants reproduce by spores.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is a mistaken negation (denying the antecedent), not a mistaken reversal; A matches the affirm-the-consequent structure exactly.

items.stimulus: If a bill has bipartisan support, it will pass. This bill lacks bipartisan support, so it will not pass.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: assumes that without the stated condition the outcome cannot occur.
takes for granted that all bills should pass.
concludes that bipartisan bills always pass instantly.
restates that the bill lacks support.
reverses the stated conditional.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: E names the wrong conditional error — this is denying the antecedent (mistaken negation, A), not a reversal.

items.stimulus: A magazine polled its readers online and found 90% support a longer school year. So most people in the country support a longer school year.
items.question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.text: The magazine's readers are mostly educators, who differ from the general public on this issue.
The poll received thousands of responses.
A longer school year would raise costs.
Some readers did not answer the poll.
Schools should survey parents directly.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: Nonresponse alone is too weak; A shows the sample is unrepresentative of the population the conclusion is about.

items.stimulus: No study has ever shown this supplement to be unsafe. Therefore, it is safe.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: treats the absence of evidence of harm as evidence of safety.
assumes the supplement is widely used.
concludes the supplement cures illness.
ignores the supplement's cost.
restates that no study found harm.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: E notes a restatement, but the defect is the inference from 'not shown unsafe' to 'safe' — an appeal to ignorance (A).

items.stimulus: Each player on the team is excellent. Therefore, the team as a whole is excellent.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: assumes that what is true of each part must be true of the whole.
presumes the players want to win.
concludes the team will win every game.
ignores the coaching staff.
restates that the players are excellent.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C attacks a prediction not made; the flaw is a part-to-whole inference (A).

items.stimulus: This year a larger percentage of the small county's residents were hospitalized than in the huge neighboring city. So the county had more hospitalizations than the city.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: confuses a higher proportion with a larger absolute number.
assumes hospitalization rates are stable.
concludes the county is less healthy overall.
ignores the reasons for hospitalization.
restates that the percentage was higher.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: E flags a restatement, but the decisive error is inferring a larger count from a larger percentage (A).

items.stimulus: Any law limiting speech is wrong, because it is wrong to limit a person's natural freedom to speak, and law is a limit on freedom.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: uses 'freedom' in two different senses across the argument.
assumes all speech is valuable.
concludes that all laws are wrong.
ignores the benefits of some speech limits.
restates that limiting freedom is wrong.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C overstates the conclusion; the actual defect is equivocation on 'freedom' (A).

items.stimulus: The new bridge will reduce commute times, because it gives drivers a shorter route downtown.
items.question: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.text: A meaningful number of drivers will actually use the shorter route.
The bridge is the shortest possible route downtown.
Commute times are the city's biggest problem.
The bridge was inexpensive to build.
Drivers dislike their current routes.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is too strong — the route need not be the shortest, only shorter; the argument only needs drivers to use it (A).

items.stimulus: Either we cut the arts budget or the school goes bankrupt. We cannot let the school go bankrupt, so we must cut the arts budget.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: presents only two options when others may be available.
assumes the arts have no value.
concludes the school is already bankrupt.
ignores how much the arts cost.
restates that bankruptcy is bad.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B imports a value claim the argument never makes; the flaw is offering a false either/or (A).

items.stimulus: My opponent wants to reduce the military budget. But leaving the nation defenseless is reckless, so her plan should be rejected.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: distorts the opponent's position into a more extreme one that is easier to attack.
relies on the opinion of an expert.
assumes the budget cannot be cut at all.
ignores the opponent's credentials.
restates that defense matters.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C misreads the conclusion; the defect is misrepresenting 'reduce' as 'leave defenseless' — a straw man (A).

items.stimulus: The scientist's argument that the lake is polluted can be dismissed. After all, she once received funding from an environmental group.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: attacks the source of the argument rather than its reasoning.
assumes the lake is definitely clean.
concludes all funded research is biased.
ignores the group's mission.
restates that she received funding.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C generalizes beyond the argument; the flaw is dismissing a claim by attacking its source (A).

items.stimulus: Offices that added indoor plants reported higher worker satisfaction. The company concludes that the plants caused the increase.
items.question: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.text: Offices otherwise identical but without added plants showed no rise in satisfaction over the same period.
Workers generally find plants pleasant to look at.
The plants were inexpensive to maintain.
Satisfaction is hard to measure precisely.
Every office should add plants.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B merely restates plausibility; A rules out an alternative explanation with a controlled comparison, strengthening the causal claim.

items.passage: For decades economists treated household saving as a purely rational response to interest rates. Behavioral researchers challenged this, arguing that habits and mental 'accounts' drive saving more than rates do. Traditional economists have not conceded the point; they respond that once uncertainty is modeled, the classical view still fits the data. A few younger scholars propose a synthesis: rates set the outer bounds of saving, while psychological factors determine where within those bounds a household lands.
items.question: The 'younger scholars' would most likely agree with which one of the following?

choices.text: Both interest rates and psychological factors shape how much households save.
Interest rates have no effect on household saving.
Behavioral research has been entirely refuted.
Saving is a purely rational response to interest rates.
Economists should abandon modeling uncertainty.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is the extreme behavioral view, not the synthesis; the younger scholars keep a role for rates (A).

items.passage: For decades economists treated household saving as a purely rational response to interest rates. Behavioral researchers challenged this, arguing that habits and mental 'accounts' drive saving more than rates do. Traditional economists have not conceded the point; they respond that once uncertainty is modeled, the classical view still fits the data. A few younger scholars propose a synthesis: rates set the outer bounds of saving, while psychological factors determine where within those bounds a household lands.
items.question: The author's attitude toward the synthesis proposed by the younger scholars is best described as

choices.text: neutral presentation without explicit endorsement or rejection.
open hostility.
unqualified enthusiasm.
dismissive skepticism.
personal regret.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: The author reports the synthesis without praising it; 'unqualified enthusiasm' overstates a neutral, descriptive tone (A).

items.passage: For decades economists treated household saving as a purely rational response to interest rates. Behavioral researchers challenged this, arguing that habits and mental 'accounts' drive saving more than rates do. Traditional economists have not conceded the point; they respond that once uncertainty is modeled, the classical view still fits the data. A few younger scholars propose a synthesis: rates set the outer bounds of saving, while psychological factors determine where within those bounds a household lands.
items.question: The mention that traditional economists 'have not conceded the point' functions primarily to

choices.text: show that the debate remained unresolved before the synthesis was offered.
prove that the behavioral researchers were mistaken.
introduce the author's own original theory.
criticize traditional economists for stubbornness.
recommend a new savings policy.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: The detail shows an ongoing standoff, not that either side was proven wrong; B distorts the author's neutral report (A).

items.stimulus: Think of the terrified families who could lose everything in a flood. Clearly, then, the proposed dam must be structurally sound.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.text: appeals to the audience's fear instead of offering evidence about the dam's construction.
assumes floods are certain to occur.
fails to define what counts as 'structurally sound'.
overlooks the cost of building the dam.
restates that families could lose everything.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C points at vagueness, but the decisive defect is substituting an emotional appeal for evidence about soundness (A).

items.stimulus: A celebrity chef says this diet is the healthiest way to eat, and she has cooked for millions. So the diet is the healthiest option for everyone.
items.question: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: treats culinary fame as if it established expertise in nutrition science.
assumes everyone has access to the diet's ingredients.
concludes the diet works for most but not all people.
ignores how much the diet costs.
restates that the chef has cooked for millions.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C misreads the conclusion, which is universal ('for everyone'); the real flaw is relying on irrelevant authority (A).

items.stimulus: This novel is the greatest of the century because no other book from these hundred years surpasses it in quality.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: supports its conclusion with a claim that merely restates that conclusion.
relies on the opinions of unnamed critics.
assumes quality can be measured objectively.
concludes that all other novels are worthless.
provides too few examples of great novels.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C raises a side assumption; the core defect is that 'greatest' and 'none surpasses it' say the same thing — circularity (A).

items.stimulus: We know the witness is telling the truth because he says he is, and an honest person would never lie about being honest.
items.question: The argument's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.text: assumes the very honesty it is trying to establish.
takes for granted that witnesses are usually reliable.
fails to consider the witness's motives.
concludes that everyone who claims honesty is honest.
ignores physical evidence in the case.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: D describes an overgeneralization, but here the premise presupposes the conclusion about this witness — a circular move (A).

items.stimulus: A four-day workweek boosted output at a small design studio. Therefore it will boost output at a large hospital.
items.question: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: assumes two very different workplaces will respond the same way to the change.
presumes the studio had no other improvements.
concludes every hospital worker will be more productive.
ignores how output is measured.
restates that output rose at the studio.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C overstates the conclusion; the defect is drawing an analogy between dissimilar settings (A).

items.stimulus: Pruning in early spring produced bigger apple harvests on our farm. Vineyards should therefore prune their grapevines in early spring to get bigger grape harvests.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: assumes apple trees and grapevines respond alike to the same pruning schedule.
takes for granted that bigger harvests are always desirable.
concludes that pruning is the only factor in harvest size.
fails to say how much bigger the apple harvest was.
restates that pruning helped the apples.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C attacks a claim the argument never makes; the flaw is assuming two different plants are relevantly comparable (A).

items.stimulus: Every rule has an exception. So the rule that every rule has an exception must itself have an exception — meaning some rule has none.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: reaches a conclusion that contradicts the premise it started from.
relies on a term, 'rule', that is never defined.
offers only one example of a rule.
assumes exceptions are always rare.
restates its premise as its conclusion.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: It is not mere restatement; the conclusion ('some rule has none') negates the opening premise — a self-contradiction (A).

items.stimulus: The committee is fully committed to open debate. Accordingly, any member who questions our recommendations will be removed.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: adopts a policy that undercuts the very commitment to open debate it professes.
assumes members will in fact raise questions.
fails to define 'open debate'.
concludes that all members disagree with the recommendations.
restates that the committee values debate.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C notes vagueness, but the flaw is that punishing dissent contradicts the stated commitment to open debate (A).

items.passage: Early histories of jazz credited a handful of famous soloists with inventing the form. Recent scholarship complicates that picture. Drawing on payroll records and club advertisements, historians now show that dozens of little-known ensemble players shaped the music's rhythmic language before any star recorded it. Some critics worry that spreading credit so widely erases genuine individual genius. The author responds that recognizing collective invention does not diminish the soloists; it simply places their achievements within the working communities that made them possible.
items.question: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.text: Newer research recasts jazz as a collective creation without denying the contributions of individual stars.
Payroll records are the most reliable source for music history.
Famous soloists deserve none of the credit once assigned to them.
Early histories of jazz contained no accurate information.
Critics have successfully refuted the new scholarship.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: The author explicitly keeps credit for soloists; C states the extreme view the author rejects, while A captures the balanced main point.

items.passage: (see rc-0100)
items.question: Which one of the following best describes the organization of the passage?

choices.text: An older view is stated, newer evidence revises it, an objection is raised, and the author answers the objection.
Two theories are presented and the first is shown to be entirely correct.
A method is described and then applied to three separate cases.
A chronological biography of a single musician is given.
A problem is posed and left deliberately unresolved.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: The author does resolve the objection in the last sentence, so it is not left open; A tracks the actual old-view/revision/objection/reply structure.

items.passage: (see rc-0100)
items.question: The passage attributes which one of the following views to the 'some critics'?

choices.text: Distributing credit among many players risks erasing individual genius.
Ensemble players contributed nothing of importance.
The new scholarship relies on unreliable sources.
Soloists should receive all of the credit and the ensembles none.
Collective invention and individual genius are fully compatible.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: E is the author's reconciling view, not the critics'; the critics fear that wide credit erases genius (A).

items.passage:
Passage A: Cities should replace downtown parking lots with housing. Land near transit is scarce, and devoting it to stored cars keeps people far from work and drives up rents. Convert the lots, and both congestion and housing costs will ease.

Passage B: Removing downtown parking sounds appealing but ignores the workers and shoppers who have no transit option. Until frequent service reaches outlying neighborhoods, stripping away parking will simply push visitors — and their business — to car-friendly suburbs.
items.question: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.text: Passage B accepts a goal Passage A shares but argues A's remedy is premature given current transit.
Passage B denies that housing costs matter at all.
The two passages address entirely unrelated policy questions.
Passage A refutes a specific study cited in Passage B.
Both passages conclude that parking lots should be preserved.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B does not reject A's aims wholesale; it objects to the timing given transit gaps, which is exactly what A recommends acting on (A).

items.passage: (see rc-0101)
items.question: The main point of Passage B is that

choices.text: converting downtown parking should wait until reliable transit serves outlying areas.
downtown parking lots should never be converted to housing.
housing costs are unrelated to the supply of land near transit.
suburban shopping is always preferable to downtown shopping.
congestion cannot be reduced by any housing policy.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B overstates B's claim into a permanent ban; the passage objects only until transit improves (A).

items.passage: (see rc-0101)
items.question: The author of Passage A would most likely regard the concern raised in Passage B as

choices.text: a consideration that a conversion plan should address rather than a reason to abandon it.
irrelevant to any question about downtown land use.
a decisive refutation of converting the lots.
evidence that housing costs cannot be lowered.
proof that transit can never be expanded.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: Passage A treats access as a problem to solve, not a fatal objection; C flips A's stance into surrender (A).

items.stimulus: Every book on the top shelf is a hardcover. The dictionary is on the top shelf.
items.question: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.text: The dictionary is a hardcover.
All hardcover books are on the top shelf.
The dictionary is the heaviest book on the shelf.
There are no paperback books anywhere in the room.
The top shelf holds only reference books.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C could be true, but nothing in the premises fixes the dictionary as the heaviest book; only its being a hardcover is guaranteed (A).

items.stimulus: All of the samples that tested positive for the enzyme came from the northern lake. Sample 12 tested positive for the enzyme.
items.question: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.text: Sample 12 came from the northern lake.
Every sample taken from the northern lake tested positive.
Sample 12 contains more of the enzyme than any other sample.
Sample 12 tested positive for the enzyme.
The northern lake is the only body of water that was sampled.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C could be true, but a positive test says nothing about relative enzyme quantity; only Sample 12's origin is forced (A).

items.stimulus: Every item in the store is either domestic or imported. No imported item is on sale this week. The blender is on sale this week.
items.question: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.text: The blender is a domestic item.
Every domestic item in the store is on sale this week.
The blender is the least expensive item in the store.
The store stocks more domestic items than imported ones.
Imported items generally cost more than domestic ones.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is too strong — the premises make the blender domestic, but say nothing that forces all domestic items onto sale (A).

items.stimulus: Since the new nutrition label was introduced, sales of high-sugar cereals have fallen every month, while sales of low-sugar cereals have risen every month. No other notable change occurred in the cereal aisle during this period.
items.question: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.text: The new nutrition label influenced at least some shoppers to choose lower-sugar cereals.
The nutrition label caused every shopper to stop buying high-sugar cereals.
High-sugar cereals will eventually vanish from the store's shelves.
Low-sugar cereals are priced lower than high-sugar cereals.
The nutrition label is now required by law.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is too strong — the data show a monthly decline, not that literally every shopper stopped; the support only reaches 'some shoppers' (A).

items.stimulus: There are more chairs than tables in the hall, and there are more tables than couches in the hall.
items.question: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.text: There are more chairs than couches in the hall.
There are exactly twice as many chairs as couches in the hall.
There is at least one couch in the hall.
There are more chairs than tables and couches combined.
Chairs are the most common piece of furniture in the whole building.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C could be true, but 'more tables than couches' is satisfied even with zero couches, so a couch is not guaranteed; only chairs > couches must hold (A).

items.stimulus: Whenever the reactor overheats, the alarm sounds. Whenever the alarm sounds, the plant shuts down. Yesterday the plant did not shut down.
items.question: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.text: The reactor did not overheat yesterday.
The reactor will never overheat again.
The alarm sounded yesterday but was ignored.
The alarm system is malfunctioning.
The reactor overheats only on rare occasions.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: D could be true, but a working chain plus 'no shutdown' only forces 'no overheat'; a malfunction is one unproven explanation, not something guaranteed (A).

items.stimulus: Last spring the city installed protected bike lanes on Elm Street. Since then the number of cyclists on Elm Street has more than doubled, while cycling on nearby streets that received no new lanes has stayed flat.
items.question: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.text: The protected bike lanes contributed to the rise in cycling on Elm Street.
Elm Street now has more cyclists than any other street in the city.
Cycling on Elm Street is now safer than driving on it.
Every resident of the city now owns a bicycle.
The nearby streets will never receive bike lanes of their own.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B could be true, but the stimulus reports a change over time on Elm Street, not a comparison of total cyclist counts across the whole city (A).

items.stimulus: Some of the volunteers are trained nurses. All trained nurses are certified in first aid.
items.question: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.text: At least some of the volunteers are certified in first aid.
All of the volunteers are certified in first aid.
Everyone certified in first aid is a volunteer.
Some of the trained nurses are not volunteers.
Most of the volunteers are trained nurses.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is too strong — only the volunteers who are nurses are guaranteed to be certified, not every volunteer (A).

items.stimulus: No mammal can breathe underwater. Every creature currently in the tank can breathe underwater. Some of the creatures in the tank are brightly colored.
items.question: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.text: Some brightly colored creatures are not mammals.
All brightly colored creatures live in the tank.
Some mammals are brightly colored.
Every creature that can breathe underwater is in the tank.
The tank contains at least one fish.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C could be true in the wider world, but nothing in the stimulus guarantees any mammal is brightly colored; the tank's colored creatures are the ones shown to be non-mammals (A).

items.stimulus: All of the coins recovered from the excavation site were minted before 200 BCE. Any coin minted before 200 BCE bears the profile of the old king.
items.question: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.text: Every coin recovered from the site bears the profile of the old king.
Every coin bearing the old king's profile was recovered from the site.
The site was inhabited before 200 BCE.
No coins anywhere were minted after 200 BCE.
The old king reigned before 200 BCE.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C could be true, but coins minted before 200 BCE could have been buried at the site much later, so habitation is not guaranteed; only the profile on the coins is forced (A).

items.stimulus: Our restaurant should add a vegan menu. A recent survey found that 40 percent of diners in our city now avoid animal products at least once a week.
items.question: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.text: At least some diners who avoid animal products would be more inclined to eat at the restaurant if it offered a vegan menu.
A majority of all diners in the city are strict vegans.
Vegan dishes are cheaper to prepare than dishes containing meat.
The restaurant currently offers no vegetarian dishes at all.
People who avoid animal products tend to live longer.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is too strong; the argument needs only that some animal-product-avoiders would respond to a vegan menu, not that most diners are strict vegans (A).

items.stimulus: The museum's attendance rose sharply after it lowered ticket prices last year. So to raise attendance still further, the museum should lower its prices again.
items.question: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.text: Some people who do not currently attend are deterred by the present ticket price.
Ticket price is the only factor that affects the museum's attendance.
Lowering prices again will not reduce the museum's total revenue.
Most current visitors first came because of the earlier price cut.
The museum's exhibits are of unusually high quality.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B is too strong; the argument requires only that price deters some potential visitors, not that price is the sole determinant of attendance (A).

items.stimulus: Ever since our town installed brighter streetlights downtown, nighttime traffic accidents there have decreased. The brighter lights are clearly responsible for the drop.
items.question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.text: During the same period the town also lowered the downtown speed limit and added crosswalks.
The brighter streetlights are more expensive to operate than the old ones.
Daytime accident rates downtown were unaffected over the same period.
Towns with brighter downtown lighting generally report fewer nighttime accidents.
A few of the newly installed streetlights occasionally flicker.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: D actually supports the causal claim (the opposite of weakening); the simultaneous speed-limit and crosswalk changes give a genuine alternative cause for the drop (A).

items.stimulus: A drug company says its new medicine is effective because 80 percent of the patients who took it recovered within a week.
items.question: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.text: Among comparable patients with the same illness who took no medicine at all, 85 percent recovered within a week.
The new medicine is more expensive than existing treatments.
A small number of patients reported mild side effects.
The study tracked each patient for a full month after recovery.
The company has successfully released several medicines in the past.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: Mild side effects don't bear on whether the drug speeds recovery; the higher no-treatment recovery rate shows the drug may add nothing (A).

items.stimulus: Office workers who kept a small plant on their desk reported less stress than workers who did not. Researchers concluded that desk plants reduce workplace stress.
items.question: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.text: When workers who previously had no desk plant were given one, their reported stress subsequently declined.
Most office workers say they enjoy having a plant nearby.
Desk plants require only minimal care to keep alive.
Workers who report less stress tend to be more productive.
The least-stressed workers in the study happened to dislike keeping plants.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: B merely restates that plants are pleasant; the before-and-after decline in stress (A) links the plants to the reduction and supports causation.

items.stimulus: I asked everyone at the yacht club whether the economy is doing well, and nearly all said yes. So the economy must be doing well for people across the whole country.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: draws a conclusion about the entire country from a group unlikely to represent it.
assumes the economy will continue to do well in the future.
concludes that every member of the yacht club is wealthy.
relies on people's opinions rather than on economic data.
restates that club members think the economy is doing well.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: Using opinions isn't itself the defect; the problem is that these opinions come from an unrepresentative group, so they can't support a nationwide claim (A).

items.stimulus: Our critics call the policy 'radical.' But radicals have always driven human progress, from scientific revolutions to social reforms. So in calling it radical, the critics have actually paid the policy a compliment.
items.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism because it

choices.text: treats two different senses of the word 'radical' as though they were one.
assumes that all progress is beneficial.
concludes that the policy will certainly succeed.
attacks the critics personally instead of their argument.
restates that the critics called the policy radical.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: The argument makes no prediction of success; its defect is shifting 'radical' from 'extreme/unconventional' to 'progress-driving' mid-argument (A).

items.stimulus: Some claim that raising the minimum wage always causes unemployment to rise. But consider Springfield: it raised its minimum wage last year, and its unemployment rate actually fell. So the claim that higher minimum wages always raise unemployment cannot be correct.
items.question: The argument proceeds by

choices.text: presenting a specific case inconsistent with a universal claim in order to refute that claim.
attacking the motives of those who make the claim.
appealing to the authority of professional economists.
showing that the claim contradicts itself.
proposing an alternative explanation for rising unemployment.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: The argument doesn't derive a contradiction from the claim itself; it supplies an external counterexample (Springfield) that the universal claim cannot accommodate (A).

items.stimulus: Lowering highway speed limits saves lives: studies consistently show that lower speeds mean fewer fatal crashes. Admittedly, lower limits also lengthen travel times. But no gain in convenience outweighs the loss of human life. The state should therefore lower the highway speed limit.
items.question: The claim that lower limits lengthen travel times plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.text: It is a consideration against the conclusion that the argument acknowledges and then sets aside.
It is the main conclusion the argument sets out to establish.
It is the primary evidence offered in support of the conclusion.
It is an assumption on which the conclusion logically depends.
It restates the argument's conclusion in different words.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: The claim isn't a needed assumption; the argument concedes it as a drawback and then outweighs it, rather than relying on it (A).

items.stimulus: If the alarm had been set, the door would have locked automatically. The door did not lock automatically. So the alarm was not set.
items.question: Which one of the following exhibits reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.text: If the sprinklers had run last night, the lawn would be wet. The lawn is not wet. So the sprinklers did not run.
If a student passes the final, she passes the course. Dana passed the final. So Dana passed the course.
If it snowed overnight, the roads were salted. The roads were salted. So it snowed overnight.
If the bakery is open, its lights are on. The bakery is not open. So its lights are not on.
All the club's members paid their dues. Sam is a member. So Sam paid his dues.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C affirms the consequent (salted, so it snowed), reversing the direction; the original and A both run validly from a denied consequent to a denied antecedent (A).

items.stimulus: After the new mayor took office, the city's crime rate dropped. Clearly, the mayor's policies reduced crime.
items.question: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.text: Shortly after the cafe started playing jazz, its sales climbed. So switching to jazz must have boosted the cafe's sales.
The cafe plays jazz and has high sales, and other jazz-playing cafes also have high sales. So jazz boosts sales.
Customers say they enjoy the cafe's jazz, so the cafe should keep playing it.
Every profitable cafe plays music, so this cafe must play music to become profitable.
The cafe has the highest sales on the street, so its jazz must be the best on the street.

assumes that all blenders require oil.
concludes that the oil is inexpensive.
ignores how often the blender is used.
restates that the driver endorses the oil.

assumes that bike lanes are inexpensive to build.
concludes that all traffic will disappear.
ignores how the bike lane will be funded.
restates that traffic fell on Maple Street.

two_answer_fork.why_runner_up_wrong: C overstates the conclusion; the defect is assuming a quiet residential street and a busy highway are relevantly alike (A).

paraphrases.stimulus: A four-day workweek worked at a small startup, so it will work at a giant factory.
paraphrases.question: The reasoning is flawed because it

items.stimulus: Every student in the room passed the exam. Priya is a student in the room.
items.question: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.text: Priya passed the exam.
Priya earned the highest score in the room.
Everyone who passed the exam is in the room.
No student outside the room passed the exam.
Priya studied hard for the exam.

paraphrases.stimulus: Every jar on the shelf is sealed. This jar is on the shelf.
